blocks.content: I've been keeping sketchbooks since I was twelve. Filled forty-three of them. My mom keeps the early ones in a bin in her closet, which I know because I found them when I was looking for my rain jacket and spent forty-five minutes on the floor reading my own handwriting from when I was fourteen. The drawings were bad. The observations in the margins were interesting. Even then, apparently, I was the kind of person who wrote notes to himself about the light.

The way I work: loose shapes first. No commitment. The street, the buildings, the suggestion of the bakery awning. I don't start with detail because detail lies — it makes you think you understand something before you've actually looked at it. I start with what a thing feels like and work backward toward what it looks like.

The street outside was doing that morning thing where everything looks slightly more itself than usual. The bookstore sign was exactly bookstore-sign blue. A woman with flowers was moving up the sidewalk — there's always a woman with flowers at this hour, different woman each time, always flowers — and the yellow she was carrying caught the east light in the exact way yellow does when the sun is still low enough to be honest.
I drew the curb. The awning. The bus stop sign.
My hand kept wanting to put her there. I redirected it twice. The third time I let it do what it wanted.
I told myself I was practicing figures. Which is true. Artists do practice figures. That is a real and legitimate thing.
I told myself this with my whole chest.
